title: Multiplayer Game
seoTitle: Design a Real-Time Multiplayer Game Backend
description: Design the backend for a real-time multiplayer game — matchmaking, dedicated game servers with fixed tick rates, client prediction and lag compensation, state synchronisation over UDP, anti-cheat, and global server fleets.
author: Editorial Team

blocks.title: What is a Multiplayer Game Backend?
blocks.text: In a real-time multiplayer game — a shooter, battle royale or racing game — players in the same match see each other move and act within tens of milliseconds. The backend matches players into games, runs an authoritative **game server** for each match that simulates the world many times per second, keeps every client's view in sync despite network lag, and stops cheaters. Turn-based games like chess are much simpler (see Online Chess).

items: Players should be matched into a game with others of similar skill and region.
Each match runs on a server that simulates the game and syncs state to all players in real time.
Players' actions (move, shoot) should feel instant, and hits should be judged fairly.
Results should update player stats and rankings after the match.

blocks.question: What are the non-functional requirements for this system?

items: Latency: round trip to the game server < 50-80 ms for most players.
Consistency: all players agree on important outcomes (who hit whom, who won).
Cheat resistance: clients can't move through walls, teleport, or see hidden information.
Scale to ~1M concurrent players in matches of 10-100, with daily peaks and launch spikes.
Perfect fairness across very different network conditions.
**Match ticket**: a player or party waiting for a match, with criteria.
**Match**: game mode, players, assigned game server, status.
**Game server**: a process on a host in a region running one or more matches.
**Snapshot**: the world state at a tick (positions, health, events).

blocks.code:
POST /matchmaking/tickets { partyId, mode, region? } -> ticketId
GET  /matchmaking/tickets/:id -> { status, server: { ip, port, token } }
UDP  client -> server: inputs { tick, buttons, aim }     (~60 per second)
UDP  server -> client: snapshots { tick, entities delta } (20-60 per second)
POST /matches/:id/results   (server -> backend)

blocks.text: Players submit **tickets** to the matchmaker, which measures each player's latency to nearby regions (pings to region beacons) and groups tickets with similar skill in the same region. The search widens gradually (skill range, regions) the longer a ticket waits. When a match is formed, it asks the **fleet allocator** for a game server.

The allocator picks a ready server in that region from a pool (pre-warmed, often on Kubernetes with Agones) and hands each player the server's address and a **join token**. Clients connect over **UDP** directly to the game server.

The game server runs a fixed **tick rate** (e.g. 30-60 Hz). Each tick it applies received player inputs, simulates physics and rules, and sends each client a **snapshot** — usually a **delta** from the last snapshot that client acknowledged, containing only entities relevant to them.
At the end of the match, the server reports results to the backend, which updates stats, ratings and rewards. The server then returns to the pool.
1) How do we make actions feel instant despite latency?

approach.text: The client sends input and only moves the character when the server's snapshot comes back.

challenges.text: Every action is delayed by a full round trip (50-150 ms) — the game feels sluggish.

approach.text: The client applies its own inputs immediately, predicting the result, and **reconciles** when the authoritative snapshot arrives: it rewinds to the server state and replays unacknowledged inputs.

challenges.text: Other players still appear jumpy, and hits on moving targets feel unfair because each player sees the world slightly in the past.

approach.text: Combine client prediction for the local player with **entity interpolation** for others (render them ~100 ms in the past, smoothly between snapshots). On the server, use **lag compensation** for hits: when a shot arrives, rewind other players to where the shooter saw them (based on the shooter's latency and interpolation delay), check the hit, then restore. The server remains authoritative throughout.

challenges.text: Rewinding must be capped (e.g. 200 ms), or high-latency players get unfair advantages ("shot behind a wall").

blocks.text: 2) How do we keep bandwidth manageable?

Sending the full world to every player 60 times a second is impossible for large matches. Use **delta compression** against acknowledged snapshots, **quantise** values (positions to centimetres, angles to a few bits), and apply **interest management**: each client only gets entities near them or in view, at lower rates for distant ones. Inputs are tiny and sent redundantly (the last few inputs in each packet) so a lost UDP packet doesn't matter.
Explain why UDP: TCP retransmits lost packets in order, so one lost packet delays everything behind it. In games, a newer snapshot makes the old one irrelevant, so we prefer losing it.

The **server is authoritative**: it validates movement (speed limits, collisions) and decides hits, so modified clients can't teleport or award themselves kills. Interest management doubles as **anti-wallhack**: clients don't receive positions of enemies they can't possibly see. Client-side anti-cheat detects memory tampering and aimbots, and server-side analytics flag statistically impossible performance for review.

quiz.question: Why do real-time games usually use UDP?
options: Lost packets aren't retransmitted, so new state isn't delayed by old state
quiz.explanation: Newer snapshots replace older ones, so waiting for retransmits hurts.

quiz.question: What is client-side prediction?
options: Applying your own inputs immediately and reconciling with the server later
quiz.explanation: It hides the round-trip delay for the local player.

quiz.question: What does lag compensation do?
options: Rewinds other players to where the shooter saw them when checking hits
quiz.explanation: It makes hits fair for players with latency.

quiz.question: How does interest management help with cheating?
options: Clients don't receive positions of enemies they can't see
quiz.explanation: Data that isn't sent can't be exploited by wallhacks.
